d2f4168868c9c9bf5764bc3a92c6399e4b6d5d1d.summary: Threat report titled 'Iron Tiger Compromises Chat Application Mimi, Targets Windows, Mac, and Linux Users'. The page is mainly an indicator-of-compromise list: SHA256 hashes for HyperBro DLL and packed payload samples (Windows) and Rshell samples (Linux and Mac OS), plus network addresses, command-and-control endpoints and download locations. The text gives no narrative on attribution, sectors, countries, CVEs or dates of activity, and it states no caveats of its own. The only dated item is the page archive date.

d26705e3fbce5f32c31647f3388f8eb19b4472df.summary: This page is a reference index for the BONDUPDATER malware family, published by Fraunhofer FKIE and archived on 2026-04-05. It lists the family's alias names (Poison Frog, Glimpse) and links it to the actors OilRig and APT34. Its reference list gives titles, dates and authors of public reports from 2018 to 2020 by various vendors and researchers. The page has no description of its own and no YARA signature. It is an index, not a threat report, so it contributes no facts.
hedges: There is no description at this point.

d21d80f8069cbea69621a907c594ab572b487c04.summary: Deep Instinct, a security vendor, analysed a Go-written variant of Micropsia, a malware used only by the Arid Viper group, which it believes is based in Gaza and calls APT-C-23. It named the new family Arid Gopher. The malware targets Windows PCs, mainly in the Middle East, and is emailed to targets in archives with a decoy document and a backdoor to a command-and-control server. Deep Instinct says Go may have been chosen to evade detection. The rest of the page is unrelated news.

d26eee9aaf68c944c7b606a24e527a22d8f044e9.summary: ANSSI's TLP:WHITE report (20/08/2020) profiles TA505, a cybercriminal group seen since at least 2014, which the report describes as a Dridex and Locky affiliate. From 2018 it moved from banking trojans and ransomware toward backdoors such as FlawedAmmyy, Get2 and SDBbot, and it deployed Clop ransomware. The report says TA505 could be a hacker-for-hire and notes possible links to Lazarus, Silence and FIN7. It also covers the Necurs botnet, which distributed much of the spam. Several attributions are hedged in the report.

d24be75959478224c4010d195a3db784a9dc56ca.summary: Trustwave SpiderLabs report on Operation Grand Mars, a campaign against hospitality organisations in Europe and the US in September and October 2016. Attacks began with phishing emails carrying macro-enabled Word documents, sometimes backed by a phone call to get the file opened. Malware used Google Docs, Google Forms and Pastebin for command and control, pass-the-hash for lateral movement, and scheduled tasks and registry autorun for persistence. Trustwave describes the operation as organised crime linked to Carbanak. The report says the certificate identities are probably fake.

hedges: The motivation of this operation appears to be financial gain, total control of the infrastructure and collection of bots.
Based on the analysis of the certificates the report says it believes the attackers purchased and used fake identities to bypass additional security controls.
The name and Russian details used in the certificate details are probably fake.
The Carbanak link rests on shared traits with the original campaign, which the report says was positively attributed to a Russian network.
The report calls the Russian/Eastern European link a weak indication, based on a Pastebin account owner's identity.
The core tools appear to comprise a variant of Anunak, a remote backdoor, plus a VBScript with data exfiltration features.
The report notes C&C servers are trivial to change, so its listed IP addresses will most likely differ in other campaigns.
The report says it does not replace formal incident response actions and procedures.
